newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU summit paves way for euro, eastern expansion.
newsitem.headline: EU summit paves way for euro, eastern expansion.

text.p: European Union leaders wound up an exuberant summit in Dublin on Saturday, driving forward plans for a future single currency and announcing a crackdown on drugs, organised crime and unemployment.

The 15-nation bloc also paved the way for an intense round of negotiations over the next six months to draw up a new EU treaty aimed at helping the Union cope with a huge influx of new members, mainly from the former communist east.
On Saturday the leaders formally endorsed a hard-won pact to make sure the future euro is as tough as the German mark, which along with most other EU currencies is to disappear with monetary union.

"The single currency is becoming a visible reality," said EU Commission President Jacques Santer after the summit had the first viewing of new euro notes due to fill the future pockets of European citizens.
With the exception of British Prime Minister John Major, EU leaders appeared in no doubt that the Dublin summit pushed forward the goal of European integration.
"I hope everyone has now understood that the caravan is moving ahead...that there is no alternative to a united Europe," said German Chancellor Helmut Kohl.
Ireland, worried about social problems at home, had been particularly eager to put down a marker on drugs, crime and unemployment, and the cause was embraced by the other EU states.
Mindful of a European jobless rate of over 10 percent, twice as high as in the United States, the leaders launched a declaration on employment, outlining steps to create new jobs.
The EU leaders also agreed a joint action plan to boost cooperation between police, customs and judicial authorities in fighting drug addiction and illegal drug trafficking.

After winding up the summit's formal business, the EU leaders turned to the thorny issue of expansion as leaders of a host of new countries clamouring to join the Union gathered in Dublin for a foretaste of EU meetings of the future.
The EU leaders met government heads from Poland, Hungary, the Czech republic, Slovakia, Slovenia, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Bulgaria, Romania and Cyprus.

Formal talks on their membership are due in about one year's time, about six months after the preparation of the new treaty needed to help the EU cope with the new members by simplifying decision-making and reducing the use of national vetoes.
The EU also wants to move forward on opening up the borders within Europe, while tightening up on security to make sure this new openness does not provide easy loopholes for criminals.
Britain's Major, whose party is deeply divided over Europe, firmly rejected the idea of giving up vetoes and opening borders. "We are not prepared to surrender the veto," he said.
Britain said it would continue to oppose many proposals in the intergovernmental conference (IGC), the negotiations for the new treaty due for approval in Amsterdam next June.
The EU also issued a hard-hitting statement, condemning Israeli settlements as a barrier to Middle East peace and calling on Yugoslavia to respect human and minority rights.
But the crowning achievement of the summit was the pact to enforce fiscal rigour and ensure the stability of the euro.
Under the deal, countries face penalties for deficits of more than three per cent of gross domestic product unless they can prove their economies are suffering a severe recession.
The accord bridged a gap between Bonn, which wanted tough terms for avoiding fines, and France, which pleaded flexibility.

But French President Jacques Chirac sowed the seed for a new Franco-German row by calling for a "political counterbalance" to a future European central bank -- anathema to Bonn which wants the bank to be as fiercely independent as its own Bundesbank.
